📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region?
  • That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.
  • Joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region? What if that developer notes that firefighters can access the pond to fight wildfires?

That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.

Joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness. The Reserve is being built on 65 acres that were once home to the Bonnie Springs Ranch, a historic, Old West-themed family resort that once featured horseback riding and a small zoo.

Two-acre empty plots in the community start at $7.5 million. But that’s not what has the community up in arms. Instead, it’s what the Reserve is touting on its website: a large human-made pond in the middle of the property.

Industry observers note that to outsiders, it seems like just one feature in a long list of amenities. But for some locals in Clark County, which was declared a natural disaster area due to drought earlier this year, the pond seems like a slap in the face—even as the developers attempt to position it as a fire safety "dip pond.".

It has been revealed that “This little dip pond here is really fire safety as an afterthought, and I think that’s pretty obvious in terms of even their planning,” remarked Sarah J. McCrea-Dameron, a Blue Diamond, NV, resident and former deputy fire chief from Las Vegas Fire & Rescue, at a zoning commission meeting this past week. “It’s not in an area that’s necessary, and it’s not the best use of that water and that precious resource for our community.“.

The Reserve at Red Rock Canyon development sits within the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area, an expansive 195,000-acre area within the Mojave Desert. Aztec sandstone foundations dating back to 180 million years can be found in the area, along with sea fossils and hundreds of local bird species. More than 3 million people visit the area each year.

Water for the area is supplied by the Colorado River. In recent years, the river and the several lakes it feeds have been pushed to the limit, as new development, coupled with more frequent droughts, have strained resources.

The river doesn’t just supply necessary water to communities across the Southwest: It also produces much-needed hydropower for the region.

Earlier this year, Lake Powell, one of the lakes fed by the Colorado River, dropped to its lowest level in history, threatening to shut down the Glen Canyon Dam, which supplies power to Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, Latest Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, and Nebraska.

Sources indicate that communities around the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area take the mantle of water conservation seriously. In fact, in 2020, the nearby community of Blue Diamond issued a temporary moratorium on “the issuance of additional water commitments” that remains in place.

Now, as the developers Laub and Jones offer unbuilt lots in their newly introduced development for $7.5 million, they are pitching the proposed pond as a neighborhood amenity.

“Paths and roads will meander past water features fed by the canyon’s natural springs,” the development’s website states.

Recent findings suggest that but those types of features are typically prohibited by Clark County’s Title 30, which governs building and development in the area. Title 30 presently prohibits the creation of human-made lakes of any size and water features greater than 10 square feet of surface area. So the developers stressed that the human-made pond would be fed via private water rights, and therefore not impede on community resources. Instead of using Colorado River resources, the project would be fed using groundwater.

It has been revealed that bob Gronauer, the developers' lawyer, said the water feature would be a “dip pond”—a water source for use by firefighting helicopters. Wildfires are a frequent problem in the region. In 2025 alone, there were 619 fires in the state, which destroyed more than 368,000 acres.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, the developers have already signed a use agreement with the Nevada Division of Forestry. The developers claimed the NDF came to them to ask them to create the pond, but the NDF said the developers approached them about the partnership, the Nevada Independent reported.

In a recent development, "We reached out to the Bureau of Land Management Red Rock management staff at the visitor center, Save Red Rock, Friends of Red Rock, as well as the Nature Conservancy Nevada immediately upon purchasing the property to work with them to make this development compatible with the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area," Laub tells Realtor.com. (Laub is the chairman of the Nature Conservancy board.).

Laub says the idea for the dip pond actually came from the BLM.

"They asked if we could work with them on fire management in Red Rock Canyon, and would we consider providing water for firefighting. Of course our answer was yes. We have a 220,000-gallon water tank designed into our water system for supplying water to our fire hydrants, and we agreed to provide a fire hydrant for the BLM water tankers to fill up in the event of a wildfire," Laub continues.

"The ponds are designed to fit into the canyon ecosystem and look natural but also to be compatible with helicopter firefighting.".

Laub tells Realtor.com that they've already been testing the wells in the canyon, and "none of the testing results from these wells has indicated a draw down of significance from our use of the water system.".

He also notes that they purchased the water rights from Bonnie Springs Ranch, which had been in use for more than 60 years.

"The property has had ponds, streams, pools, and springs from the original ranch in 1952," he explains.

To expedite the creation of the dip pools, the developers proposed an amendment to Title 30 that would add language permitting “a body of water, served from standalone private water rights, within 1,000 feet of a National Conservation Area, intended for fire suppression and life safety purposes as agreed upon with a State or Federal Agency.”In October, Clark County Planning Commission's professional staff recommended denying the amendment.

Recent findings suggest that "As proposed, there is no indication of how these water features would be designed, the capacity of these water features, or other potential uses for the stored water. The proliferation of non-essential water features will place an additional burden on the existing water supply," the staff recommendation read. "Furthermore, this request may encourage additional non-essential water features within residential and nonresidential development.".

It has been revealed that however, the Planning Commission approved the amendment by a vote of 6-1. It then went to the Clark County Zoning Board for approval. On Wednesday night, during the public comment period of the meeting, around a dozen community members spoke out against the planned feature.

In a recent development, “You can design a decorative water feature and then call it a dip pond. You can offer to let the Forest Service use it knowing that they never will because of the way it’s designed and location, but that doesn’t make that decorative water feature a piece of critical fire infrastructure," stated former Clark County Fire Capt. Erik Klausen.

“They’re trying to put a plastic fire helmet on this water feature and tell us it’s about public safety,” he continued.

At the end of the public comment period, all seven commissioners voted in favor of the proposed amendment, though, as Commissioner Justin Jones noted, the approval of the amendment does not mean the dip pond project has been approved.

Furthermore, noted Commissioner Marilyn Kirkpatrick, the project needs to be fit for purpose.

Sources indicate that "If it's a fire-suppression pond, then it has to be a fire-suppression pond in my mind," stated Kirkpatrick. "It should stay as a fire-supression pond, not as a recreational venue, not as irrigation, because that water is supposed to be there for a reason.".

Realtor.com has reached out to developer Jones and lawyer Gronauer for comment.

She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

Industry observers note that eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

In a recent development, engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the firm.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Sources indicate that realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the organization. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa mentioned in a statement.

Sources indicate that rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Sources indicate that jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Recent findings suggest that baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

It has been revealed that IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl remarked in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter stated in a statement.

Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it.
  • Recent findings suggest that that shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure.
  • “Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:46 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Industry observers note that agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

Recent findings suggest that that shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

“Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill mentioned.

Cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

Agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

“There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill mentioned.

In a recent development, security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

“I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill said. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the confidentiality, without breaching one another.”.

The same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.’s VMware business. That lets enterprises run old and newly introduced applications on one general-purpose platform, Cantrill noted.

In a recent development, “You want all that flexibility that you get from elastic compute, but you need it for economic reasons, security reasons, latency reasons,” Cantrill said of the case for on-premises cloud computing. “You need it in your own data center. You want to control your fate.”.

#30345. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

Industry observers note that this is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

Recent findings suggest that in their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

Industry observers note that the millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

Recent findings suggest that “For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s vital to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

It has been revealed that millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another major expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

In a recent development, adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

It has been revealed that baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

In a recent development, but their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

According to recent reports, “The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao mentioned. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

That dynamic highlights up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners remarked they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

Recent findings suggest that this analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Recent findings suggest that home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

According to recent reports, monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Recent findings suggest that share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

According to recent reports, how to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report reveals each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

In a recent development, it’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

Sources indicate that to leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

It has been revealed that season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

Recent findings suggest that at the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio stated the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He mentioned he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Sources indicate that I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”.

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Sources indicate that alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

It has been revealed that alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Industry observers note that alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Pete Dadds / FOX. ©2026 FOX Media LLC.as.

Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she mentioned to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”.

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

Sources indicate that and each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Industry observers note that alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a significant hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”.

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Pete Dadds / FOX. ©2026 FOX Media LLC.as.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

Industry observers note that I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a massive, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Recent findings suggest that mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

It has been revealed that I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

Traveling Home for Thanksgiving? How Smart Buyers Turn Holiday Visits Into Neighborhood Recon

💡 Key Takeaways
  • That’s why it’s no surprise that the latest Migration Trends report by the National Association of Realtors® found that 30% of buyers who relocated did so to be near family.
  • Whether the goal is to care for aging parents, assist with childcare, or simply enjoy more time with loved ones, living near family can make a positive difference in everyday life.
  • If you’ve been contemplating buying a home closer to family, your Thanksgiving visit could be the perfect opportunity to start exploring what life in a newly introduced area could look like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For most people, family is everything.

That’s why it’s no surprise that the latest Migration Trends report by the National Association of Realtors® found that 30% of buyers who relocated did so to be near family.

Whether the goal is to care for aging parents, assist with childcare, or simply enjoy more time with loved ones, living near family can make a positive difference in everyday life.

If you’ve been contemplating buying a home closer to family, your Thanksgiving visit could be the perfect opportunity to start exploring what life in a newly introduced area could look like.

Since you’re already making the trip, it only makes sense to get a firsthand look at the neighborhoods, homes, and local amenities to help you determine whether the move is worthwhile for your budget and lifestyle.

“Seeing how a community operates when people are home, traffic is heavier, and daily routines are stressed can help you make an informed decision about where to plant roots,” states Cameron Walker, real estate expert and manager of the agent network at Clever Real Estate in St. Louis.

Once you arrive in town for Thanksgiving, take a commute during rush hour.

Then, walk around the area during the day and at night and check out local shops, restaurants, parks, and other attractions.

“Be sure to speak to locals about traffic, parking, safety, noise, and other concerns that might arise during different seasons,” indicates Walker.

Pay attention to all the small details that will matter if you make the move: sidewalk length and quality, road conditions, street parking availability, cell service reliability, distance to the nearest airport, and proximity to hospitals.

If you have time, you may also want to attend a few open houses and meet with a real estate agent.

“Look at homes for sale, recent home sales, and the length of time homes are taking to sell, as well as how many price reductions are being made. Learn about local property taxes, insurance costs, and whether there are many homes for sale that fit your price range,” Walker adds.

In addition, focus on schools, childcare, commute times, and other amenities to make sure you’d feel comfortable with your daily routines.

In a recent development, in the late fall and early winter, typical buyer activity drops off sharply in many markets. That’s why it’s a great time to look for a home.

Depending on the market, it may open the doors to some unique negotiation leverage.

“As fewer and fewer buyers are ‘in the market’ from Thanksgiving to the Newly introduced Year, sellers may become more flexible in their terms,” states Sander Scott, owner and broker of Net Real Estate in Traverse City, MI.

And there may be even more opportunities this year.

According to the Realtor.com® October 2026 housing report, approximately 1 in 5 listings had a price reduction, while active inventory was up 7.4% compared to last year.

That means you might have more housing options at your disposal and sellers may be more willing to adjust their asking prices.

Industry observers note that “Focus on the right location and daily function. After all, saving money on a house that makes the childcare or caregiving goal harder to achieve defeats the purpose,” Scott adds.

In addition, think of a refinance as a potential bonus—not your plan.

Industry observers note that “Rates come and go, but the purchase price is forever. Always consider the purchase price, the monthly payment, and whether you can afford it in the long run,” explains Walker.

Look beyond the monthly mortgage payment and understand the total cost of ownership. Being close to family is no fun if it forces you to become house poor as a result.

“Thanksgiving is about catching up with family members and eating turkey, but it may also be about seeing if a relocation is feasible for your particular financial situation,” Walker adds.

According to recent reports, last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

Industry observers note that the Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

In a recent development, finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

According to recent reports, chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople.
  • It has been revealed that I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since.
  • It has been revealed that the reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

It has been revealed that I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

It has been revealed that the reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

According to recent reports, nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

Industry observers note that this isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

It has been revealed that we do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

Sources indicate that what would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

Industry observers note that there’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

According to recent reports, that work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

Recent findings suggest that we haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

Industry observers note that if you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

Industry observers note that you aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

XRP Ledger Foundation Director of Community Hussein Zangana (Vet) shared a tidbit of XRPL's early history in a recent X post.

Vet noted that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) still carries traces of Satoshi Nakamoto’s original Bitcoin design, highlighting two features.

In 2011, three engineers—David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto—began developing the XRP Ledger (XRPL). Fascinated by Bitcoin, they set out to create a better version that improved upon its limitations—with the goal of creating a digital asset that was more sustainable and built specifically for payments.

As reported, the first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written by David Schwartz, who is Ripple CTO emeritus, about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011.

Industry observers note that vet delves into the earliest part of XRP Ledger history, noting that 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, wrote. Vet added that Jed McCaleb also copied Satoshi’s timekeeping code into the XRPL, even including one of the Bitcoin creator’s comments shared as a screenshot.

It has been revealed that did you know all of us on the XRP Ledger use design choices by Satoshi daily? 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Satoshi wrote. Jed copied Satoshi's timekeeping code into the XRPL, including one of Satoshi's comments. By the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone. In December 2014, Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment. Two design choices of Satoshi still remain on the XRPL and all of us use at least one of it. Signature curve secp256k1 (we also support Ed25519 thus not everyone uses this) and how XRPL addresses are generated from the public key with SHA-256 followed by RIPEMD-160, that's what all of us use.

The quote "Never go to sea with two chronometers; take one or three" is a classic maritime adage famously included by Satoshi Nakamoto (the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin) within the Bitcoin source code.

Vet explained that by the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone from the XRP Ledger. In December 2014, former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment.

However, two of Satoshi's design choices still remain on the XRP Ledger: the first is the secp256k1 signature curve, which Bitcoin uses and which the XRP Ledger continues to support. However, the ledger also supports Ed25519, meaning not every XRPL user relies on secp256k1.

"I remember David saying they used secp256k1 so no one would doubt the security because it's the same as Bitcoin's, etc.," Vet stated, citing the insight of the Ripple CTO emeritus on secp256k1, adding, "Lots of interesting things to dig into from the early days.".

It has been revealed that the second is the method used to generate XRP Ledger addresses from public keys. The process applies SHA-256 hashing followed by RIPEMD-160, a design inherited from Bitcoin that remains common to all XRPL addresses.

Asked why the timekeeping code and Satoshi's comment were removed, Vet explained that this became leftover code as upcoming code was introduced, so it was cleaned up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s upcoming monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

According to recent reports, lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

In a recent development, debt was a major part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on newly introduced real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb looks to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the organization noted in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

It has been revealed that instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment problems, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

It has been revealed that “Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”.

Industry observers note that the announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first unveiled in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

It has been revealed that preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”.

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve.".

Industry observers note that the vote closed on Nov. 15, and DReps holding 2.86 billion ADA voted against the proposal, according to Cardano governance data. DReps with 20.02 million ADA voted in favor of it.

DRep John MacPherson was among those who voted "No," and he explained his decision in a post on X.

MacPherson wrote that he is not against real-world assets on Cardano. Still, he remarked the proposal asks the treasury "to take on both the copper price and the ada price," and Toto Finance would collect "up to about 3.4M ada in fees.".

At the same time, MacPherson said that the proposal is “more honest about its risks than most.”.

Toto Finance, a company led by Monty Metzger, submitted the proposal on Oct. 15. ADA is trading at $0.152 on Monday, and the requested 22 million ADA is now worth around $3.3 million.

The plan was to buy copper with 14.72 million ADA and store it in a warehouse near Latest Orleans. Toto Finance wanted to problem one CuTT token for each pound of copper. The metal would be sold in 18 to 24 months.

The Cardano Foundation, which votes as a DRep, declared its "No" vote in October.

"We recognize the opportunity in real-world asset tokenization; however, this proposal places 22,000,000 ada under the recipient's sole control to fund a fee-heavy concentrated commodity position whose safeguards are not yet in place," the foundation wrote.

Three members of the Constitutional Committee voted "No," and the other four members did not vote.

Crypto commentator Ingeniero Cripto agreed with MacPherson in the replies under his post. He called the "double exposure" to the prices of copper and ADA the key problem of the proposal, as the Cardano treasury already holds ADA.

According to him, RWAs on Cardano make sense, but “funding the asset itself is a different question than funding the rails.”.

Melania Trump has given another look into her life as first lady with the premiere of “Melania: The Series,” a two-episode follow-up to the previously released "Melania" documentary.

Both the film and the series detail the weeks leading up to President Donald Trump’s January 2025 inauguration.

Recent findings suggest that in the first episode, which was released on Nov. 20, Melania prepares to resume her White House duties for a second term.

“The role of the first lady is managing of the White House,” she explained. “And I think people don’t realize that the first lady is in charge of the residence.”.

She spoke at length about her approach to the role, noting the pride she takes in carrying out duties such as decorating the Washington, DC, landmark and planning events.

“I’m proud to elevate America through every detail brought to life within the White House,” noted Melania. “Each event is carefully planned for months with the design, decor, cuisine, music, and atmosphere, all arranged with precision to showcase our nation’s beauty, strength, and grace.”.

Melania explained that her hope is for “the White House to showcase the greatness of American culture,” and that she wanted to elevate it “to the highest standard.”.

According to recent reports, “We preserve. We restore. We build latest stuff,” she noted. “The White House should be the best of the best. It represents our country.”.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 6, the president declared the Oval Office a national monument in an attempt to prevent future presidents from making changes to the renovations that have been made in his second term.

According to recent reports, “We’ve had tremendous victory in this office,” he said. “So we’re making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape.”.

The White House has undergone extensive work since Trump has reentered office, including an overhaul of the iconic Rose Garden and a destruction of the East Wing to accommodate proposed plans for a 90,000-square-foot ballroom.

The first lady explained that she’s always had an interest in interior design, and when asked what kind of career she might have pursued had she not began working as a model before meeting her now-husband.

Sources indicate that “I would continue studying architecture. I think I would do something with design,” she stated. Melania had briefly attended the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia, where she studied the design discipline before leaving after a few months to pursue modeling.

She also revealed that she had aims to bring some of her own pieces back to the White House.

According to recent reports, “I will make it a home again,” she mentioned. “Last time was very beautiful, very comfortable. We all loved it, and we will do it again.”.

At one point, an off-screen interviewer notes that “so much thought” goes into each minute decision and asks Melania, “Does your husband recognize the detail?”.

According to recent reports, “He takes the whole experience in. He’s busy with his own job, and his mind’s going nonstop,” she said. “He has so much to take care of. So maybe he doesn’t realize how much work it is.”.

At another moment in the documentary, Melania hinted at the scope of her role, saying, “I know what my husband is doing and what my son is doing, but I don’t think they know what I’m doing.”.

Ahead of the inauguration, CNN reported that Melania would most likely not reside in the White House full time, which she appeared to confirm in the docuseries.

It has been revealed that “My home is in three cities. Each has purpose and serves varying parts of my life,” she said. “To balance this lifestyle, I’m very intentional and detail-oriented.”.

Aside from the White House, the Melania splits her time between Trump Tower in New York City and Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, FL.

She also expressed how much she values privacy, noting the importance of getting enough sleep and seeking “solitude.”.

“I don’t need to be all the time with people,” said Melania. “I’m very happy in my own organization. I always was.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Industry observers note that existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant stated she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant remarked mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Sources indicate that added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

Sources indicate that as a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

Recent findings suggest that “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he stated. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

Sources indicate that “If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale stated existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

According to recent reports, “Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

It has been revealed that “[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she noted. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun stated rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the significant change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

Sources indicate that however, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on newly introduced pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”.
